title: Level 11 — Academic Independence & Synthesis
_generificationNote: L11 v2.1: factual generification applied from the start. No specific dated studies, sample sizes, or effect sizes that could not be independently verified appear in any item. Broad research claims use defensible phrasings such as 'research consistently finds...' or 'reviews of X have reported...'. Well-documented historical facts and major-source figures (Ireland 2002 bag charge ~90% drop, IRENA solar cost falls, FAO ~14.5% livestock emissions, OECD ~9% recycled plastic, IPCC AR6 1.1°C, EU 2013 cosmetics ban, Mueller & Oppenheimer 2014 in Psychological Science, Kisida 2014 art-museum study, Pontevedra 1999, Tallinn 2013, Beland & Murphy 2015 LSE working paper, Australian compulsory voting, Perry Preschool follow-up, Scottish Referendum Study 2014 Eichhorn turnout figures) appear where directly relevant. _needsReview flags appear on L11.C1 only because it is a Phase 1 visual-pending skill per the blueprint; the flag tracks visual-upgrade status, not factual content.

grammarRules.pronounReference: checked for ambiguity in extended writing

academicRegisterRules.slang: rejected ('kid', 'kinda', 'gonna', 'stuff', 'like' as filler, 'you know', 'super' as intensifier)
academicRegisterRules.firstPersonInformal: rejected as the default voice; 'I argue' / 'I contend' / 'in my view' acceptable in formal essays only when prompt invites them
academicRegisterRules.secondPerson: avoided in academic essays; acceptable in oral presentations addressed to an audience
academicRegisterRules.casualConnectives: rejected ('also', 'plus' as stand-alone connectors); academic alternatives required ('furthermore', 'moreover', 'in addition')
academicRegisterRules.vagueQuantifiers: softened ('a lot', 'tons of', 'loads of' → 'a substantial number of', 'many', 'a significant share')

contexts.A: Single extended text — used for rhetorical analysis (L11.A3) and oral text evaluation (L11.D3).
contexts.B: Two texts on the same topic — used for conflict reconciliation (L11.A2).
contexts.C: Three or more sources — used for synthesis (L11.A1) and research summary (L11.B1).

masteryRules: 3 correct demonstrations per skill · at least 2 contexts · at least 2 non-consecutive sessions · academic register and citation language maintained throughout.

ERR_MULTI_SOURCE_SYNTHESIS.description: Three-source synthesis not integrated or not attributed

variants.SOURCE_MISSING_L11: One of the 3 sources not referenced.
variants.PARALLEL_SUMMARY_L11: Three separate summaries rather than one integrated response. Integration Cohesion <0.40 (RED zone).
variants.ATTRIBUTION_ABSENT_L11: A claim is made in the research summary without attribution to any source.
variants.VERBATIM_RESEARCH: Copying score ≥65% per sentence in research summary.
variants.PARALLEL_RESEARCH: Three sources described in isolation rather than synthesized.

ERR_CONFLICTING_INFO.description: Conflicting information not identified or reconciled

variants.CONTRADICTION_MISSED: Learner does not identify the specific conflicting claims across the two texts.
variants.REASON_ABSENT_L11: Contradiction identified but no explanation for the difference offered.
variants.REASON_DISMISSIVE: Reason given as 'one text is wrong' — does not engage with the substance of the difference.

ERR_RHETORICAL_AWARENESS.description: Rhetorical or structural choices not explained

variants.CHOICE_NOT_IN_TEXT_L11: Named structural or rhetorical choice not present in the given text.
variants.EFFECT_VAGUE_L11: Effect described without a specific purpose verb.
variants.CHOICE_NOT_LINKED: Choice identified but not linked to the text's overall purpose.

ERR_CITATION_LANGUAGE.description: Formal citation language absent or mismatched

variants.CITATION_ABSENT_L11: A sourced claim has no attribution phrase.
variants.CITATION_MISMATCH_L11: Citation phrase used does not match the type of source use (introduces/quotes/summarises).
variants.CITATION_WITHOUT_SOURCE: Citation phrase used with no identifiable source reference.

variants.WEAK_THESIS_L11: Thesis breadth <0.40 — does not cover the scope of the essay.
variants.NO_CEE_BODY_L11: Body paragraph missing one or more CEE components.
variants.TRANSITION_ABSENT_L11: Paragraph transitions absent or wrong function.
variants.MISSING_CONCLUSION_L11: Essay ends without a conclusion paragraph.
variants.REGISTER_COLLAPSE_L11: Casual register detected in any paragraph.

ERR_SELF_EVALUATION.description: Cannot identify logical gaps or unsupported claims in own writing

variants.GAP_NOT_REAL: Identified logical gap is not a gap — the argument is coherent at that point.
variants.UNSUPPORTED_NOT_REAL: Identified unsupported claim actually has evidence nearby.
variants.SELF_EVAL_VAGUE: Weakness identified without naming a specific paragraph or sentence.
variants.CRITERION_MISSED: Learner fails to flag a paragraph that genuinely fails a criterion (Phase 1 checklist variant).
variants.FALSE_POSITIVE: Learner flags a passing paragraph as failing a criterion (Phase 1 checklist variant).

variants.REVISION_SURFACE_ONLY: Revision changes sentence structure only — evidence not strengthened, logic not improved.
variants.EVIDENCE_NOT_STRENGTHENED: Revised draft shows no improvement in evidence keyword overlap with source text.
variants.NO_IMPROVEMENT: Coherence score unchanged or lower after revision (RED zone).

ERR_ORAL_PRESENTATION.description: Formal presentation missing required structural components

variants.NO_PREVIEW_INTRO: Introduction does not preview the main points.
variants.NO_EVIDENCE_POINT_L11: A body point contains no evidence reference.
variants.TIMING_FAIL: Presentation under 2:30 min or over 6:00 min.
variants.CASUAL_REGISTER_PRESENTATION: Contraction or slang in any section of the presentation.

ERR_QA_EVIDENCE.description: Cannot respond to Q&A with evidence from presentation

variants.QUESTION_EVADED: Response does not address the question that was asked.
variants.NO_EVIDENCE_QA: Response given without any evidence reference from the presentation.
variants.SHORT_QA_RESPONSE: Fewer than 2 complete clauses in the Q&A response.
variants.CASUAL_REGISTER_QA: Contraction or informal word in Q&A response.
variants.ARGUMENT_MISSED_L11: Overall argument not stated before evaluation begins (L11.D3).
variants.NO_EVIDENCE_EVAL_L11: Evaluation does not assess any specific piece of evidence (L11.D3).
variants.NO_VERDICT: Evaluation ends without a reasoned judgment on the text's persuasiveness.

recoveryActions.SOURCE_MISSING_L11: source map: one key point per source confirmed before writing.
recoveryActions.NO_ATTRIBUTION_L11: citation audit: every sourced claim must be attributed before resubmission.
recoveryActions.PARALLEL_SUMMARY_L11: integration frame: learner writes one sentence referencing all three sources before drafting the full synthesis. Frame removed after 3 passing responses.
recoveryActions.ATTRIBUTION_ABSENT_L11: citation audit enforced before each submission.
recoveryActions.VERBATIM_RESEARCH: system hides sources before writing summary.
recoveryActions.PARALLEL_RESEARCH: integration frame: write one sentence linking all three sources before the summary.
recoveryActions.CONTRADICTION_MISSED: contradiction mapping: system presents the two contradictory claims as labelled text blocks. Learner writes one sentence naming the specific point of difference.
recoveryActions.REASON_ABSENT_L11: reason framework: 'Why might two sources say different things about the same topic?'
recoveryActions.REASON_DISMISSIVE: reason framework with substantive options: different data, time period, perspective, or methodology.
recoveryActions.CHOICE_NOT_IN_TEXT_L11: evidence-first: highlight the feature in the text before naming it.
recoveryActions.EFFECT_VAGUE_L11: purpose-verb list: creates / reinforces / emphasises / suggests / positions.
recoveryActions.CHOICE_NOT_LINKED: sentence frame: 'This [choice] serves the author's purpose to [PURPOSE] because ___.'
recoveryActions.CITATION_ABSENT_L11: citation audit of own writing before submission: every sourced claim must be checked and attributed.
recoveryActions.CITATION_MISMATCH_L11: citation function chart with examples of each type (introduces / quotes / summarises).
recoveryActions.CITATION_WITHOUT_SOURCE: remove the citation phrase or add a source reference.
recoveryActions.WEAK_THESIS_L11: reverse drill: write body paragraphs first, then write the thesis.
recoveryActions.NO_CEE_BODY_L11: CEE rebuild: paragraph reframed with claim / evidence / explanation prompts.
recoveryActions.TRANSITION_ABSENT_L11: transition audit: system highlights every paragraph boundary; learner writes one connecting sentence at each boundary. Essay accepted only after all transitions are function-matched.
recoveryActions.MISSING_CONCLUSION_L11: system requires a conclusion paragraph referencing the thesis with no new arguments.
recoveryActions.REGISTER_COLLAPSE_L11: immediate rejection; learner replaces flagged words before resubmission.
recoveryActions.CRITERION_MISSED: Guided criterion-by-criterion drill: system presents one paragraph and one criterion at a time. Learner applies just that criterion and records PASS or FAIL with paragraph number.
recoveryActions.FALSE_POSITIVE: system explains why the flagged paragraph passes the criterion.
recoveryActions.SELF_EVAL_VAGUE: system requires: 'Write the paragraph number and the first three words of the sentence that causes the failure.'
recoveryActions.REVISION_SURFACE_ONLY: focused revision protocol: one evidence task + one transition task per session only.
recoveryActions.EVIDENCE_NOT_STRENGTHENED: system shows the weakest evidence sentence; learner replaces it with a stronger evidence sentence from the source.
recoveryActions.NO_IMPROVEMENT: system highlights two sentences at the paragraph boundary; learner writes one new transition sentence connecting them.
recoveryActions.NO_PREVIEW_INTRO: presentation structure template: four-section outline with required components per section.
recoveryActions.NO_EVIDENCE_POINT_L11: evidence-link prompt: 'Which part of your source supports this point?'
recoveryActions.MISSING_CONCLUSION_ORAL_L11: system prompts for a closing paragraph referencing the opening.
recoveryActions.TIMING_FAIL: timed practice protocol with mid-point flag.
recoveryActions.CASUAL_REGISTER_PRESENTATION: register checklist before next attempt; flagged words replaced.
recoveryActions.QUESTION_EVADED: Q&A frame: 'The question asks about [X]. In my presentation I showed [EVIDENCE]. This means [ANSWER].'
recoveryActions.NO_EVIDENCE_QA: 'Which part of your presentation supports this answer?'
recoveryActions.ARGUMENT_MISSED_L11: evaluation frame: 'This text argues [X]. The evidence includes [A] which is [strong/weak] because [REASON]. Overall, I find this [convincing/unconvincing] because [REASON].'
recoveryActions.NO_EVIDENCE_EVAL_L11: evaluation frame: each evidence assessment must name a specific quality criterion.
recoveryActions.NO_VERDICT: 'What is your final judgment on the text?'

skills.skillName: Synthesize information from ≥3 texts into a single integrated response

items.passage:
Source 1 — AAP policy position
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The recommendation cites the adolescent shift in circadian rhythms: teenagers, on average, fall asleep and wake later than younger children, and very early start times are associated with insufficient sleep. Pilot districts that have moved their start times later report attendance and sleep-duration gains and reductions in teen-driver crash rates. The AAP frames its recommendation as a public-health intervention, not merely an educational change.

Source 2 — Logistical objection
School administrators in many regions raise practical objections to later start times. Bus rotations, after-school sport schedules, working-parent drop-offs, and elementary-school timings are all affected when high schools shift their start times. A 2019 review by district administrators argued that the costs of restructuring transport alone can be substantial, and that the benefits of later start times — while well-documented at the individual level — must be weighed against community-wide disruption.

Source 3 — Outcomes from changed districts
Where districts in the United States have made the shift to start times of 8:30 a.m. or later, follow-up reports tend to describe a consistent pattern: pupils report more sleep on school nights, on-time attendance improves, and teen-driver crash rates in those districts fall. School administrators in changed districts also report that initial transport-restructuring costs are typically absorbed within one to two academic years, and that the wellbeing improvements outweigh the early administrative burden.
items.prompt: You will see three short sources on the topic of school start times for teenagers. Write ONE integrated paragraph (120–180 words) that synthesizes the information across all three sources. Use attribution phrases for each source ('Source 1 reports...', 'Source 2 argues...', 'Source 3 finds...' or equivalents). Do NOT write three separate summaries.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Phone-ban evidence
Beland and Murphy's 2015 LSE Centre for Economic Performance working paper on phone bans reported modest test-score gains in schools that introduced phone bans, with the largest gains for lower-attaining pupils. The authors framed phones as a source of in-class distraction whose removal levels the playing field, helping pupils whose home circumstances may already make focused study harder.

Source 2 — Educational-use argument
Some educators argue that outright phone bans are blunt instruments that ignore the genuine educational uses of personal devices. Phones can support translation for English-language learners, on-the-fly research, classroom polling, accessibility tools for pupils with reading difficulties, and contact with parents in emergencies. These educators advocate structured phone policies — phones away during instruction, available during set research activities — rather than blanket bans.

Source 3 — Lockable-pouch policy outcomes
Schools that have introduced phone-removal policies, often using lockable pouches at the school entrance, have reported modest gains in classroom focus and test performance, alongside declines in lunch-time conflicts that originated in social-media exchanges. Several head teachers describe the policy as easier to enforce than partial rules, because the device is physically inaccessible during the school day rather than relying on pupil self-control during lessons.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Pontevedra case study
When Pontevedra in Spain closed its centre to private cars in 1999, the share of children walking to school rose sharply, air pollution measurably improved, and small shops in the pedestrian zone reported steady or rising takings. The city has since maintained the policy and reports a substantial fall in city-centre traffic deaths. Pontevedra is widely cited in urban-policy discussions as an early example of a small city demonstrating that pedestrianisation does not destroy local commerce.

Source 2 — Retailer objection
Independent retailer organisations in several countries have raised concerns about pedestrianisation. They argue that customers who arrive by car typically buy more in a single visit than walkers do, and that lost car access depresses sales for shops selling bulky goods. They also note that pedestrianisation often follows infrastructure decisions made by city planners without retailer consultation, and that the cost of adaptation falls on small businesses rather than on the planners who design the scheme.

Source 3 — Long-term outcomes
Long-term studies of pedestrianised European city centres have generally reported that, after an initial adjustment period, shop takings hold up or rise. Foot traffic increases, residents report higher satisfaction with the centre, and tourism in pedestrianised areas tends to grow. Researchers in this area emphasise that outcomes depend strongly on transport alternatives — good public transport and clear loading-bay provision for deliveries make pedestrianisation easier to absorb than abrupt closures with no replacement infrastructure.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Carbon-pricing case
Economists working on climate policy have generally argued that placing a price on carbon emissions — either through a tax or a tradable-permit scheme — is among the most economically efficient ways to reduce emissions. The IPCC AR6 working-group reports identify carbon pricing as a useful policy lever where political conditions allow. The argument rests on the idea that polluters internalise costs they otherwise externalise onto society, and that the resulting price signal lets firms and consumers find their own least-costly emission cuts.

Source 2 — Distributional objection
Critics of carbon pricing argue that, in practice, the policy can be regressive: lower-income households spend a larger share of income on energy and basic goods, so a flat carbon price falls hardest on those least able to absorb it. Several jurisdictions have introduced dividend-style rebates to offset this effect, returning revenue directly to households. Without such rebates, critics warn, carbon pricing risks generating political backlash that undermines the longer-term effort, as the 2018 gilets jaunes protests in France illustrated.

Source 3 — Outcome reports
Jurisdictions that have implemented carbon-pricing schemes report mixed but generally encouraging outcomes. The EU Emissions Trading System, in place since 2005, has been associated with measurable emission reductions in the covered sectors, particularly after reforms tightened the cap in the 2010s. British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax, also widely studied, has been associated with reduced fuel consumption without a significant negative effect on overall economic growth. Researchers in this area generally conclude that well-designed carbon-pricing schemes — particularly those that recycle revenue to households or low-carbon investment — can be both environmentally effective and economically defensible.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Emissions case for reducing meat
The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that livestock production accounts for about 14.5 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, with beef and lamb among the most emission-intensive foods per kilogram. Reports such as the EAT-Lancet Commission's 2019 publication argue that, on a global level, reducing average meat consumption — particularly red and processed meat — is one of the more impactful individual actions available for emission reduction, and that this shift would also tend to improve population health outcomes.

Source 2 — Cultural and economic objection
Farmers' organisations and rural communities in many countries argue that headline 'reduce meat' messages overlook important context. Pastoral grazing on uplands that cannot grow crops, regenerative grazing systems that build soil carbon, and small-scale livestock production that supports rural employment all complicate the simple argument that less meat is always better. These organisations call for nuanced policy that distinguishes among production systems rather than treating all meat as interchangeable in environmental impact.

Source 3 — Public-health outcomes
Major public-health bodies, including the World Health Organization, have linked high consumption of processed meat to increased cardiovascular and colorectal-cancer risk. Country-level dietary guidelines in the Nordic region, the Netherlands, and the UK have for several years recommended moderate, rather than high, meat consumption. Researchers caution that effective public-health messaging in this area must balance health evidence with respect for cultural practices and economic realities, and that prescriptive guidance is more likely to be ignored than nuanced, context-sensitive recommendations.

items.passage:
Source 1 — AI-tutoring case
Published research from Stanford's Graduate School of Education on AI tutoring has reported measurable test-score gains for well-designed AI-tutoring interventions, with effect sizes varying widely by study and implementation. The most consistent finding across the literature is that AI tutors are most useful as a supplement to human teaching — particularly for spaced practice, immediate feedback, and questions whose answers depend on consistent application of stated rules — rather than as a replacement for the teacher's role.

Source 2 — Equity and access objection
Critics of widespread classroom AI adoption argue that the benefits of AI tools depend heavily on home infrastructure: reliable broadband, suitable devices, and adult supervision are uneven across socio-economic groups. Without deliberate equity measures, AI tools risk widening rather than narrowing existing gaps. Critics also point to data-protection concerns when children's writing, queries, and learning records pass through private servers, particularly where vendor practices on data retention and resale are opaque.

Source 3 — Implementation findings
Schools that have implemented AI tutoring at scale tend to report that the most consistent benefits arise when AI is integrated into existing curricula rather than added as a separate activity, when teachers actively shape what AI is asked to do, and when pupils have stable access at home as well as at school. Implementation reports emphasise that the technology itself is rarely the determining factor: design choices, teacher training, and equity policy together account for the variation in outcomes between successful and unsuccessful programmes.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Helmet case
Reviews of cycle-helmet research have consistently found substantial reductions in serious head injuries among helmet wearers compared with non-wearers in equivalent crash scenarios. Helmets are widely cited by public-health bodies as one of the most cost-effective individual protective interventions available to cyclists, and many jurisdictions either mandate them for children or strongly recommend them for all riders.

Source 2 — Infrastructure-first counter-case
Critics of mandatory adult helmet laws argue that, while helmets reduce individual injury risk in a crash, compulsory laws can reduce cycling participation overall — and that lower participation worsens public health in the aggregate. The Netherlands and Denmark, which have very high cycling rates and very low cycling-injury rates, have not introduced compulsory helmet laws; instead, they have built extensive protected cycle infrastructure. Critics frame infrastructure investment as the more effective long-run safety lever.

Source 3 — Comparative country outcomes
Cross-country comparisons of cyclist-safety outcomes suggest that countries with the safest cycling environments tend to combine well-designed infrastructure, lower urban speed limits, and strong driver-awareness norms, with or without compulsory helmet laws. Researchers in this area generally argue that helmet wearing and infrastructure investment are complements rather than substitutes — that the goal of cyclist safety is best served by a combination of personal protection where appropriate and systemic change to roads and traffic culture.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Library funding case
Independent valuation studies have estimated that every pound spent on public and school libraries returns several pounds in measurable social and educational value through improved literacy, employment support, and community wellbeing. School-library research in the United States and the United Kingdom has also linked staffed school libraries with higher reading-attainment scores, particularly among pupils from lower-income backgrounds whose home access to books is limited.

Source 2 — Digital-substitution argument
Some commentators argue that, in the age of widespread internet access, dedicated school libraries are a less essential resource than they once were. They point to free online texts, e-book lending services, and search engines as substitutes for physical library collections. From this perspective, dedicated library staff and physical book collections compete for school budgets that could otherwise be spent on classroom technology or additional teaching hours.

Source 3 — Equity and quiet-space argument

Published research from Stanford's Graduate School of Education on AI tutoring has reported measurable test-score gains for well-designed AI-tutoring interventions, with effect sizes varying widely by study and implementation. Critics of widespread classroom AI adoption argue that the benefits of AI tools depend heavily on home infrastructure: reliable broadband, suitable devices, and adult supervision are uneven across socio-economic groups. Without deliberate equity measures, AI tools risk widening rather than narrowing existing gaps. Critics also point to data-protection concerns when children's writing, queries, and learning records pass through private servers, particularly where vendor practices on data retention and resale are opaque.

Source 3 — Implementation findings
Schools that have implemented AI tutoring at scale tend to report that the most consistent benefits arise when AI is integrated into existing curricula rather than added as a separate activity, when teachers actively shape what AI is asked to do, and when pupils have stable access at home as well as at school. Implementation reports emphasise that the technology itself is rarely the determining factor: design choices, teacher training, and equity policy together account for the variation in outcomes between successful and unsuccessful programmes.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The recommendation cites the adolescent shift in circadian rhythms: teenagers, on average, fall asleep and wake later than younger children, and very early start times are associated with insufficient sleep. School administrators in changed districts also report that initial transport-restructuring costs are typically absorbed within one to two academic years, and that the wellbeing improvements outweigh the early administrative burden.

When Pontevedra in Spain closed its centre to private cars in 1999, the share of children walking to school rose sharply, air pollution measurably improved, and small shops in the pedestrian zone reported steady or rising takings. The city has since maintained the policy and reports a substantial fall in city-centre traffic deaths. Pontevedra is widely cited in urban-policy discussions as an early example of a small city demonstrating that pedestrianisation does not destroy local commerce.

Independent retailer organisations in several countries have raised concerns about pedestrianisation. They argue that customers who arrive by car typically buy more in a single visit than walkers do, and that lost car access depresses sales for shops selling bulky goods. They also note that pedestrianisation often follows infrastructure decisions made by city planners without retailer consultation, and that the cost of adaptation falls on small businesses rather than on the planners who design the scheme.

Source 3 — Long-term outcomes
Long-term studies of pedestrianised European city centres have generally reported that, after an initial adjustment period, shop takings hold up or rise. Foot traffic increases, residents report higher satisfaction with the centre, and tourism in pedestrianised areas tends to grow. Researchers in this area emphasise that outcomes depend strongly on transport alternatives — good public transport and clear loading-bay provision for deliveries make pedestrianisation easier to absorb than abrupt closures with no replacement infrastructure.

Without such rebates, critics warn, carbon pricing risks generating political backlash that undermines the longer-term effort, as the 2018 gilets jaunes protests in France illustrated.

Jurisdictions that have implemented carbon-pricing schemes report mixed but generally encouraging outcomes. The EU Emissions Trading System, in place since 2005, has been associated with measurable emission reductions in the covered sectors, particularly after reforms tightened the cap in the 2010s. British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax, also widely studied, has been associated with reduced fuel consumption without a significant negative effect on overall economic growth. Researchers in this area generally conclude that well-designed carbon-pricing schemes — particularly those that recycle revenue to households or low-carbon investment — can be both environmentally effective and economically defensible.

Recent meta-analyses of homework research conclude that regular short homework tasks, particularly in mathematics and language subjects, are associated with measurable improvements in pupil attainment when set at an age-appropriate level. The authors of one widely-cited review argue that homework develops self-regulated study habits and that the largest gains accrue to pupils who would otherwise have little time for review at home. Several education ministries have, on the basis of this body of research, recommended structured homework in secondary schools.

Source 2 — Homework worsens equity
A separate strand of research on homework reports a different conclusion. Studies focused on pupils from lower-income households find that homework can entrench rather than reduce attainment gaps, because pupils without quiet study space, parental help, or reliable broadband cannot complete homework on the same terms as wealthier peers. The authors of these studies argue that, for pupils without home support, homework time displaces sleep, family interaction, or paid work, and that the net effect on learning is negative once those displacement costs are taken into account.

The authors who hold this view point to a strong correlation between time spent on screens and self-reported mental ill-health, particularly among adolescent girls. From this perspective, the medium is less important than the design quality and the reader's habits.

items.passage:
Source 1 — The case for compulsory cycling infrastructure
Every year, the same headlines return: another cyclist killed by a heavy goods vehicle on a city street, another inquest, another statement of regret. And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Consider the Netherlands. Consider Denmark. Consider, increasingly, parts of Belgium, parts of Germany, parts of Spain. What do these countries have in common? Not compulsory helmet laws. Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. What they have is infrastructure — protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by kerbs and bollards, designed for ordinary people on ordinary bikes going at ordinary speeds. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The argument that personal protective equipment is the answer puts the responsibility on the cyclist. But the cyclist is not the problem. The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell swimmers to be careful around boats in a harbour; we forbid swimming there. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Helmets help in individual crashes. The evidence is clear on that. But individual helmets do not stop the next inquest, because helmets do not change the conditions that produce inquests. Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Against the digitisation of the classroom
Walk into a state-of-the-art classroom in any wealthy country and you will see the same thing: rows of children in front of glowing rectangles. The rectangles are praised. They are interactive. They are engaging. They are the future. They are also, increasingly, evidence that we have got something seriously wrong.

Consider what learning actually requires. It requires sustained attention. It requires the ability to hold an idea in mind long enough to do something difficult with it. It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

The defenders of classroom digitisation point to the genuine educational uses of technology — and there are some. A spreadsheet for a science investigation is a useful tool. A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. What fills the average classroom screen is what fills every other screen in the child's life: notifications, half-finished thoughts, the gentle ache of interruption that we have all come to accept as the price of being conscious in our century.

There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

Schools that have removed phones from classrooms tend to report what one might predict: a quieter room, longer attention on a single task, easier teacher-led discussion, calmer corridors at break. These are not small things. These are the substrate of education. We removed it. We can put it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. items.passage:
Source 1 — The case for compulsory cycling infrastructure
Every year, the same headlines return: another cyclist killed by a heavy goods vehicle on a city street, another inquest, another statement of regret. And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Consider the Netherlands. Consider Denmark. Consider, increasingly, parts of Belgium, parts of Germany, parts of Spain. What do these countries have in common? Not compulsory helmet laws. Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. What they have is infrastructure — protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by kerbs and bollards, designed for ordinary people on ordinary bikes going at ordinary speeds. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The argument that personal protective equipment is the answer puts the responsibility on the cyclist. But the cyclist is not the problem. The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell swimmers to be careful around boats in a harbour; we forbid swimming there. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Helmets help in individual crashes. The evidence is clear on that. But individual helmets do not stop the next inquest, because helmets do not change the conditions that produce inquests. Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Against the digitisation of the classroom
Walk into a state-of-the-art classroom in any wealthy country and you will see the same thing: rows of children in front of glowing rectangles. The rectangles are praised. They are interactive. They are engaging. They are the future. They are also, increasingly, evidence that we have got something seriously wrong.

Consider what learning actually requires. It requires sustained attention. It requires the ability to hold an idea in mind long enough to do something difficult with it. It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

The defenders of classroom digitisation point to the genuine educational uses of technology — and there are some. A spreadsheet for a science investigation is a useful tool. A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. What fills the average classroom screen is what fills every other screen in the child's life: notifications, half-finished thoughts, the gentle ache of interruption that we have all come to accept as the price of being conscious in our century.

There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

Schools that have removed phones from classrooms tend to report what one might predict: a quieter room, longer attention on a single task, easier teacher-led discussion, calmer corridors at break. These are not small things. These are the substrate of education. We removed it. We can put it back.

And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Against the digitisation of the classroom

It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Against the digitisation of the classroom
Walk into a state-of-the-art classroom in any wealthy country and you will see the same thing: rows of children in front of glowing rectangles. The rectangles are praised. They are interactive. They are engaging. They are the future. They are also, increasingly, evidence that we have got something seriously wrong.

Consider what learning actually requires. It requires sustained attention. It requires the ability to hold an idea in mind long enough to do something difficult with it. It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

The defenders of classroom digitisation point to the genuine educational uses of technology — and there are some. A spreadsheet for a science investigation is a useful tool. A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. What fills the average classroom screen is what fills every other screen in the child's life: notifications, half-finished thoughts, the gentle ache of interruption that we have all come to accept as the price of being conscious in our century.

There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

Schools that have removed phones from classrooms tend to report what one might predict: a quieter room, longer attention on a single task, easier teacher-led discussion, calmer corridors at break. These are not small things. These are the substrate of education. We removed it. We can put it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

items.passage:
Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — The case for compulsory cycling infrastructure
Every year, the same headlines return: another cyclist killed by a heavy goods vehicle on a city street, another inquest, another statement of regret. And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Consider the Netherlands. Consider Denmark. Consider, increasingly, parts of Belgium, parts of Germany, parts of Spain. What do these countries have in common? Not compulsory helmet laws. Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. What they have is infrastructure — protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by kerbs and bollards, designed for ordinary people on ordinary bikes going at ordinary speeds. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The argument that personal protective equipment is the answer puts the responsibility on the cyclist. But the cyclist is not the problem. The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell swimmers to be careful around boats in a harbour; we forbid swimming there. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Helmets help in individual crashes. The evidence is clear on that. But individual helmets do not stop the next inquest, because helmets do not change the conditions that produce inquests. Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

items.passage:
Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — AAP policy position
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The recommendation cites the adolescent shift in circadian rhythms: teenagers, on average, fall asleep and wake later than younger children, and very early start times are associated with insufficient sleep. Pilot districts that have moved their start times later report attendance and sleep-duration gains and reductions in teen-driver crash rates. The AAP frames its recommendation as a public-health intervention, not merely an educational change.

Source 2 — Logistical objection
School administrators in many regions raise practical objections to later start times. Bus rotations, after-school sport schedules, working-parent drop-offs, and elementary-school timings are all affected when high schools shift their start times. A 2019 review by district administrators argued that the costs of restructuring transport alone can be substantial, and that the benefits of later start times — while well-documented at the individual level — must be weighed against community-wide disruption.

Source 3 — Outcomes from changed districts
Where districts in the United States have made the shift to start times of 8:30 a.m. or later, follow-up reports tend to describe a consistent pattern: pupils report more sleep on school nights, on-time attendance improves, and teen-driver crash rates in those districts fall. School administrators in changed districts also report that initial transport-restructuring costs are typically absorbed within one to two academic years, and that the wellbeing improvements outweigh the early administrative burden.

Source 1 — Phone-ban evidence
Beland and Murphy's 2015 LSE Centre for Economic Performance working paper on phone bans reported modest test-score gains in schools that introduced phone bans, with the largest gains for lower-attaining pupils. The authors framed phones as a source of in-class distraction whose removal levels the playing field, helping pupils whose home circumstances may already make focused study harder.

Source 2 — Educational-use argument
Some educators argue that outright phone bans are blunt instruments that ignore the genuine educational uses of personal devices. Phones can support translation for English-language learners, on-the-fly research, classroom polling, accessibility tools for pupils with reading difficulties, and contact with parents in emergencies. These educators advocate structured phone policies — phones away during instruction, available during set research activities — rather than blanket bans.

Source 3 — Lockable-pouch policy outcomes
Schools that have introduced phone-removal policies, often using lockable pouches at the school entrance, have reported modest gains in classroom focus and test performance, alongside declines in lunch-time conflicts that originated in social-media exchanges. Several head teachers describe the policy as easier to enforce than partial rules, because the device is physically inaccessible during the school day rather than relying on pupil self-control during lessons.

Source 1 — Pontevedra case study
When Pontevedra in Spain closed its centre to private cars in 1999, the share of children walking to school rose sharply, air pollution measurably improved, and small shops in the pedestrian zone reported steady or rising takings. The city has since maintained the policy and reports a substantial fall in city-centre traffic deaths. Pontevedra is widely cited in urban-policy discussions as an early example of a small city demonstrating that pedestrianisation does not destroy local commerce.

Source 2 — Retailer objection
Independent retailer organisations in several countries have raised concerns about pedestrianisation. They argue that customers who arrive by car typically buy more in a single visit than walkers do, and that lost car access depresses sales for shops selling bulky goods. They also note that pedestrianisation often follows infrastructure decisions made by city planners without retailer consultation, and that the cost of adaptation falls on small businesses rather than on the planners who design the scheme.

Source 3 — Long-term outcomes
Long-term studies of pedestrianised European city centres have generally reported that, after an initial adjustment period, shop takings hold up or rise. Foot traffic increases, residents report higher satisfaction with the centre, and tourism in pedestrianised areas tends to grow. Researchers in this area emphasise that outcomes depend strongly on transport alternatives — good public transport and clear loading-bay provision for deliveries make pedestrianisation easier to absorb than abrupt closures with no replacement infrastructure.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Carbon-pricing case
Economists working on climate policy have generally argued that placing a price on carbon emissions — either through a tax or a tradable-permit scheme — is among the most economically efficient ways to reduce emissions. The IPCC AR6 working-group reports identify carbon pricing as a useful policy lever where political conditions allow. The argument rests on the idea that polluters internalise costs they otherwise externalise onto society, and that the resulting price signal lets firms and consumers find their own least-costly emission cuts.

Source 2 — Distributional objection
Critics of carbon pricing argue that, in practice, the policy can be regressive: lower-income households spend a larger share of income on energy and basic goods, so a flat carbon price falls hardest on those least able to absorb it. Several jurisdictions have introduced dividend-style rebates to offset this effect, returning revenue directly to households. Without such rebates, critics warn, carbon pricing risks generating political backlash that undermines the longer-term effort, as the 2018 gilets jaunes protests in France illustrated.

Source 3 — Outcome reports
Jurisdictions that have implemented carbon-pricing schemes report mixed but generally encouraging outcomes. The EU Emissions Trading System, in place since 2005, has been associated with measurable emission reductions in the covered sectors, particularly after reforms tightened the cap in the 2010s. British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax, also widely studied, has been associated with reduced fuel consumption without a significant negative effect on overall economic growth. Researchers in this area generally conclude that well-designed carbon-pricing schemes — particularly those that recycle revenue to households or low-carbon investment — can be both environmentally effective and economically defensible.
