items.passage:
Source 1 — The case for compulsory cycling infrastructure
Every year, the same headlines return: another cyclist killed by a heavy goods vehicle on a city street, another inquest, another statement of regret. And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Consider the Netherlands. Consider Denmark. Consider, increasingly, parts of Belgium, parts of Germany, parts of Spain. What do these countries have in common? Not compulsory helmet laws. Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. What they have is infrastructure — protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by kerbs and bollards, designed for ordinary people on ordinary bikes going at ordinary speeds. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The argument that personal protective equipment is the answer puts the responsibility on the cyclist. But the cyclist is not the problem. The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell swimmers to be careful around boats in a harbour; we forbid swimming there. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Helmets help in individual crashes. The evidence is clear on that. But individual helmets do not stop the next inquest, because helmets do not change the conditions that produce inquests. Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

items.passage:
Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Against the digitisation of the classroom
Walk into a state-of-the-art classroom in any wealthy country and you will see the same thing: rows of children in front of glowing rectangles. The rectangles are praised. They are interactive. They are engaging. They are the future. They are also, increasingly, evidence that we have got something seriously wrong.

Consider what learning actually requires. It requires sustained attention. It requires the ability to hold an idea in mind long enough to do something difficult with it. It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

The defenders of classroom digitisation point to the genuine educational uses of technology — and there are some. A spreadsheet for a science investigation is a useful tool. A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. What fills the average classroom screen is what fills every other screen in the child's life: notifications, half-finished thoughts, the gentle ache of interruption that we have all come to accept as the price of being conscious in our century.

There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

Schools that have removed phones from classrooms tend to report what one might predict: a quieter room, longer attention on a single task, easier teacher-led discussion, calmer corridors at break. These are not small things. These are the substrate of education. We removed it. We can put it back.

items.passage:
Source 1 — Why universal public services matter
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

items.passage:
Source 1 — In defence of boredom
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.
items.prompt:
You will see an extended text (400–600 words) titled 'In defence of boredom'. Deliver a structured oral evaluation. Your evaluation must contain:
(1) Overall argument: state the text's main argument in one sentence at the start.
(2) Evidence assessment 1: identify one piece of evidence in the text and assess its     quality using a specific criterion (specificity, relevance, recency,     representativeness, methodology, source credibility, scale, comparability).
(3) Evidence assessment 2: identify a second piece of evidence and assess its quality     using a specific criterion (it can be the same criterion type or a different one).
(4) Verdict: give a reasoned final judgment on the text's persuasiveness, with a     'because' clause that ties the verdict to your evidence assessments.
Total length: at least 6 complete clauses across the four components. Academic register throughout.
items.question: Evaluate 'In defence of boredom' orally using the four-component structure above.

checks.description: Overall argument of the text is stated in one sentence at or near the start of the evaluation. Failure triggers ARGUMENT_MISSED_L11.

At least 2 evidence assessments, each naming a specific piece of evidence from the text AND a specific quality criterion (specificity, relevance, recency, representativeness, methodology, source credibility, scale, comparability). Bare 'this evidence is weak/strong' without a named criterion fails. Failure triggers NO_EVIDENCE_EVAL_L11.
Final verdict is present — a reasoned judgment on the text's persuasiveness with a 'because' clause linking the verdict to the evidence assessments. Failure triggers NO_VERDICT.
Evaluation contains at least 6 complete clauses across the four components. Fewer triggers SHORT_EVALUATION_L11.
No contractions, no slang, no informal first-person filler. CASUAL_REGISTER_EVAL triggered on first violation.

texts.label: AAP policy position
texts.passage: The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The recommendation cites the adolescent shift in circadian rhythms: teenagers, on average, fall asleep and wake later than younger children, and very early start times are associated with insufficient sleep. Pilot districts that have moved their start times later report attendance and sleep-duration gains and reductions in teen-driver crash rates. The AAP frames its recommendation as a public-health intervention, not merely an educational change.

Pilot districts that have moved their start times later report attendance and sleep-duration gains and reductions in teen-driver crash rates. The AAP frames its recommendation as a public-health intervention, not merely an educational change.

texts.label: Logistical objection
texts.passage: School administrators in many regions raise practical objections to later start times. Bus rotations, after-school sport schedules, working-parent drop-offs, and elementary-school timings are all affected when high schools shift their start times. A 2019 review by district administrators argued that the costs of restructuring transport alone can be substantial, and that the benefits of later start times — while well-documented at the individual level — must be weighed against community-wide disruption.

texts.label: Outcomes from changed districts
texts.passage: Where districts in the United States have made the shift to start times of 8:30 a.m. or later, follow-up reports tend to describe a consistent pattern: pupils report more sleep on school nights, on-time attendance improves, and teen-driver crash rates in those districts fall. School administrators in changed districts also report that initial transport-restructuring costs are typically absorbed within one to two academic years, and that the wellbeing improvements outweigh the early administrative burden.

texts.label: Phone-ban evidence
texts.passage: Beland and Murphy's 2015 LSE Centre for Economic Performance working paper on phone bans reported modest test-score gains in schools that introduced phone bans, with the largest gains for lower-attaining pupils. The authors framed phones as a source of in-class distraction whose removal levels the playing field, helping pupils whose home circumstances may already make focused study harder.

texts.label: Educational-use argument
texts.passage: Some educators argue that outright phone bans are blunt instruments that ignore the genuine educational uses of personal devices. Phones can support translation for English-language learners, on-the-fly research, classroom polling, accessibility tools for pupils with reading difficulties, and contact with parents in emergencies. These educators advocate structured phone policies — phones away during instruction, available during set research activities — rather than blanket bans.

texts.label: Lockable-pouch policy outcomes
texts.passage: Schools that have introduced phone-removal policies, often using lockable pouches at the school entrance, have reported modest gains in classroom focus and test performance, alongside declines in lunch-time conflicts that originated in social-media exchanges. Several head teachers describe the policy as easier to enforce than partial rules, because the device is physically inaccessible during the school day rather than relying on pupil self-control during lessons.

texts.label: Pontevedra case study
texts.passage: When Pontevedra in Spain closed its centre to private cars in 1999, the share of children walking to school rose sharply, air pollution measurably improved, and small shops in the pedestrian zone reported steady or rising takings. The city has since maintained the policy and reports a substantial fall in city-centre traffic deaths. Pontevedra is widely cited in urban-policy discussions as an early example of a small city demonstrating that pedestrianisation does not destroy local commerce.

Pontevedra is widely cited in urban-policy discussions as an early example of a small city demonstrating that pedestrianisation does not destroy local commerce.

texts.label: Retailer objection
texts.passage: Independent retailer organisations in several countries have raised concerns about pedestrianisation. They argue that customers who arrive by car typically buy more in a single visit than walkers do, and that lost car access depresses sales for shops selling bulky goods. They also note that pedestrianisation often follows infrastructure decisions made by city planners without retailer consultation, and that the cost of adaptation falls on small businesses rather than on the planners who design the scheme.

texts.label: Long-term outcomes
texts.passage: Long-term studies of pedestrianised European city centres have generally reported that, after an initial adjustment period, shop takings hold up or rise. Foot traffic increases, residents report higher satisfaction with the centre, and tourism in pedestrianised areas tends to grow. Researchers in this area emphasise that outcomes depend strongly on transport alternatives — good public transport and clear loading-bay provision for deliveries make pedestrianisation easier to absorb than abrupt closures with no replacement infrastructure.

texts.label: Carbon-pricing case
texts.passage: Economists working on climate policy have generally argued that placing a price on carbon emissions — either through a tax or a tradable-permit scheme — is among the most economically efficient ways to reduce emissions. The IPCC AR6 working-group reports identify carbon pricing as a useful policy lever where political conditions allow. The argument rests on the idea that polluters internalise costs they otherwise externalise onto society, and that the resulting price signal lets firms and consumers find their own least-costly emission cuts.

The IPCC AR6 working-group reports identify carbon pricing as a useful policy lever where political conditions allow. The argument rests on the idea that polluters internalise costs they otherwise externalise onto society, and that the resulting price signal lets firms and consumers find their own least-costly emission cuts.

texts.label: Distributional objection
texts.passage: Critics of carbon pricing argue that, in practice, the policy can be regressive: lower-income households spend a larger share of income on energy and basic goods, so a flat carbon price falls hardest on those least able to absorb it. Several jurisdictions have introduced dividend-style rebates to offset this effect, returning revenue directly to households. Without such rebates, critics warn, carbon pricing risks generating political backlash that undermines the longer-term effort, as the 2018 gilets jaunes protests in France illustrated.

texts.label: Outcome reports
texts.passage: Jurisdictions that have implemented carbon-pricing schemes report mixed but generally encouraging outcomes. The EU Emissions Trading System, in place since 2005, has been associated with measurable emission reductions in the covered sectors, particularly after reforms tightened the cap in the 2010s. British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax, also widely studied, has been associated with reduced fuel consumption without a significant negative effect on overall economic growth. Researchers in this area generally conclude that well-designed carbon-pricing schemes — particularly those that recycle revenue to households or low-carbon investment — can be both environmentally effective and economically defensible.

texts.label: Emissions case for reducing meat
texts.passage: The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that livestock production accounts for about 14.5 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, with beef and lamb among the most emission-intensive foods per kilogram. Reports such as the EAT-Lancet Commission's 2019 publication argue that, on a global level, reducing average meat consumption — particularly red and processed meat — is one of the more impactful individual actions available for emission reduction, and that this shift would also tend to improve population health outcomes.

texts.label: Cultural and economic objection
texts.passage: Farmers' organisations and rural communities in many countries argue that headline 'reduce meat' messages overlook important context. Pastoral grazing on uplands that cannot grow crops, regenerative grazing systems that build soil carbon, and small-scale livestock production that supports rural employment all complicate the simple argument that less meat is always better. These organisations call for nuanced policy that distinguishes among production systems rather than treating all meat as interchangeable in environmental impact.

These organisations call for nuanced policy that distinguishes among production systems rather than treating all meat as interchangeable in environmental impact.

texts.label: Public-health outcomes
texts.passage: Major public-health bodies, including the World Health Organization, have linked high consumption of processed meat to increased cardiovascular and colorectal-cancer risk. Country-level dietary guidelines in the Nordic region, the Netherlands, and the UK have for several years recommended moderate, rather than high, meat consumption. Researchers caution that effective public-health messaging in this area must balance health evidence with respect for cultural practices and economic realities, and that prescriptive guidance is more likely to be ignored than nuanced, context-sensitive recommendations.

texts.label: AI-tutoring case
texts.passage: Published research from Stanford's Graduate School of Education on AI tutoring has reported measurable test-score gains for well-designed AI-tutoring interventions, with effect sizes varying widely by study and implementation. The most consistent finding across the literature is that AI tutors are most useful as a supplement to human teaching — particularly for spaced practice, immediate feedback, and questions whose answers depend on consistent application of stated rules — rather than as a replacement for the teacher's role.

texts.label: Equity and access objection
texts.passage: Critics of widespread classroom AI adoption argue that the benefits of AI tools depend heavily on home infrastructure: reliable broadband, suitable devices, and adult supervision are uneven across socio-economic groups. Without deliberate equity measures, AI tools risk widening rather than narrowing existing gaps. Critics also point to data-protection concerns when children's writing, queries, and learning records pass through private servers, particularly where vendor practices on data retention and resale are opaque.

texts.label: Implementation findings
texts.passage: Schools that have implemented AI tutoring at scale tend to report that the most consistent benefits arise when AI is integrated into existing curricula rather than added as a separate activity, when teachers actively shape what AI is asked to do, and when pupils have stable access at home as well as at school. Implementation reports emphasise that the technology itself is rarely the determining factor: design choices, teacher training, and equity policy together account for the variation in outcomes between successful and unsuccessful programmes.

texts.label: Helmet case
texts.passage: Reviews of cycle-helmet research have consistently found substantial reductions in serious head injuries among helmet wearers compared with non-wearers in equivalent crash scenarios. Helmets are widely cited by public-health bodies as one of the most cost-effective individual protective interventions available to cyclists, and many jurisdictions either mandate them for children or strongly recommend them for all riders.

Helmets are widely cited by public-health bodies as one of the most cost-effective individual protective interventions available to cyclists, and many jurisdictions either mandate them for children or strongly recommend them for all riders.

texts.label: Infrastructure-first counter-case
texts.passage: Critics of mandatory adult helmet laws argue that, while helmets reduce individual injury risk in a crash, compulsory laws can reduce cycling participation overall — and that lower participation worsens public health in the aggregate. The Netherlands and Denmark, which have very high cycling rates and very low cycling-injury rates, have not introduced compulsory helmet laws; instead, they have built extensive protected cycle infrastructure. Critics frame infrastructure investment as the more effective long-run safety lever.

The Netherlands and Denmark, which have very high cycling rates and very low cycling-injury rates, have not introduced compulsory helmet laws; instead, they have built extensive protected cycle infrastructure. Critics frame infrastructure investment as the more effective long-run safety lever.

texts.label: Comparative country outcomes
texts.passage: Cross-country comparisons of cyclist-safety outcomes suggest that countries with the safest cycling environments tend to combine well-designed infrastructure, lower urban speed limits, and strong driver-awareness norms, with or without compulsory helmet laws. Researchers in this area generally argue that helmet wearing and infrastructure investment are complements rather than substitutes — that the goal of cyclist safety is best served by a combination of personal protection where appropriate and systemic change to roads and traffic culture.

texts.label: Library funding case
texts.passage: Independent valuation studies have estimated that every pound spent on public and school libraries returns several pounds in measurable social and educational value through improved literacy, employment support, and community wellbeing. School-library research in the United States and the United Kingdom has also linked staffed school libraries with higher reading-attainment scores, particularly among pupils from lower-income backgrounds whose home access to books is limited.

School-library research in the United States and the United Kingdom has also linked staffed school libraries with higher reading-attainment scores, particularly among pupils from lower-income backgrounds whose home access to books is limited.

texts.label: Digital-substitution argument
texts.passage: Some commentators argue that, in the age of widespread internet access, dedicated school libraries are a less essential resource than they once were. They point to free online texts, e-book lending services, and search engines as substitutes for physical library collections. From this perspective, dedicated library staff and physical book collections compete for school budgets that could otherwise be spent on classroom technology or additional teaching hours.

From this perspective, dedicated library staff and physical book collections compete for school budgets that could otherwise be spent on classroom technology or additional teaching hours.

texts.label: Equity and quiet-space argument
texts.passage: Researchers studying the role of school libraries note that the case for them rests less on book provision alone than on three combined functions: a quiet supervised study space for pupils whose home does not provide one, expert guidance on reading from a qualified school librarian, and equity of access to curated material that the open internet does not provide. From this perspective, online substitutes address only one of the three functions, leaving the equity and guidance functions weakened in schools that have closed their libraries.

From this perspective, online substitutes address only one of the three functions, leaving the equity and guidance functions weakened in schools that have closed their libraries.

texts.label: Homework supports learning
texts.passage: Recent meta-analyses of homework research conclude that regular short homework tasks, particularly in mathematics and language subjects, are associated with measurable improvements in pupil attainment when set at an age-appropriate level. The authors of one widely-cited review argue that homework develops self-regulated study habits and that the largest gains accrue to pupils who would otherwise have little time for review at home. Several education ministries have, on the basis of this body of research, recommended structured homework in secondary schools.

Several education ministries have, on the basis of this body of research, recommended structured homework in secondary schools.

texts.label: Homework worsens equity
texts.passage: A separate strand of research on homework reports a different conclusion. Studies focused on pupils from lower-income households find that homework can entrench rather than reduce attainment gaps, because pupils without quiet study space, parental help, or reliable broadband cannot complete homework on the same terms as wealthier peers. The authors of these studies argue that, for pupils without home support, homework time displaces sleep, family interaction, or paid work, and that the net effect on learning is negative once those displacement costs are taken into account.

texts.label: Screen time harms wellbeing
texts.passage: Researchers including Dr Jean Twenge have argued that depression and anxiety rates among US adolescents began climbing in the early 2010s, coinciding with the rapid adoption of smartphones and social-media platforms. The authors who hold this view point to a strong correlation between time spent on screens and self-reported mental ill-health, particularly among adolescent girls. From this perspective, large platform companies bear significant responsibility for current trends in adolescent wellbeing.

The authors who hold this view point to a strong correlation between time spent on screens and self-reported mental ill-health, particularly among adolescent girls. From this perspective, large platform companies bear significant responsibility for current trends in adolescent wellbeing.

texts.label: Screen-time effect overstated
texts.passage: Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute and elsewhere have published findings consistent with a 'Goldilocks' hypothesis: moderate use of digital devices is associated with about the same — or marginally higher — life satisfaction than no use at all, with negative effects emerging only at very high levels of use. From this perspective, the headline claim that screen time is destroying adolescent mental health is overstated, and the wider effect sizes in the literature are small once researcher freedom is accounted for. The researchers argue that other social changes during the 2010s — economic instability, climate anxiety, the rise of high-stakes testing — likely matter more than screen time alone.

texts.label: Minimum-wage rises cost jobs
texts.passage: A long-standing strand of labour economics, exemplified by Neumark and colleagues, finds that increases in the minimum wage reduce employment among the least-skilled workers — particularly teenagers, recent immigrants, and those in regions where average wages are already low. The authors argue that, while higher minimum wages benefit workers who keep their jobs, the policy harms those at the very margin of the labour market who lose them, and that the net effect on low-income households is therefore uncertain or negative.
texts.topic: the employment effect of the minimum wage
texts.body: A long-standing strand of labour economics, exemplified by Neumark and colleagues, finds that increases in the minimum wage reduce employment among the least-skilled workers — particularly teenagers, recent immigrants, and those in regions where average wages are already low. The authors argue that, while higher minimum wages benefit workers who keep their jobs, the policy harms those at the very margin of the labour market who lose them, and that the net effect on low-income households is therefore uncertain or negative.

texts.label: Minimum-wage rises broadly neutral on jobs
texts.passage: A different and equally substantial strand of labour economics, originating with Card and Krueger's 1994 study of New Jersey fast-food employment, finds little or no employment effect from moderate minimum-wage increases. More recent natural-experiment studies in Seattle and elsewhere have produced similar conclusions for the range of increases observed. The authors argue that, in real labour markets, employers face frictions that allow them to absorb modest wage increases through productivity gains, slightly higher prices, or reduced employer profits, rather than through cuts to employment.

texts.label: Organic better for biodiversity
texts.passage: A long-running body of agricultural research has reported that organic farming systems — defined by their restrictions on synthetic pesticide and fertiliser use — support higher biodiversity per hectare than comparable conventional systems. The authors cite higher counts of pollinator species, wild plants, and soil organisms in organic fields, and argue that, on biodiversity grounds, expansion of organic farming would benefit broader ecosystem health.
texts.topic: organic versus conventional farming for the environment
texts.body: A long-running body of agricultural research has reported that organic farming systems — defined by their restrictions on synthetic pesticide and fertiliser use — support higher biodiversity per hectare than comparable conventional systems. The authors cite higher counts of pollinator species, wild plants, and soil organisms in organic fields, and argue that, on biodiversity grounds, expansion of organic farming would benefit broader ecosystem health.

texts.label: Organic worse on land use
texts.passage: A separate body of agricultural research, focused on yield rather than per-hectare biodiversity, reaches a more critical conclusion. Organic systems typically produce lower yields per hectare than conventional systems for the same crops, meaning that producing the same total quantity of food organically requires substantially more land. The authors argue that, on a global scale, expanding organic farming would push agriculture into forests, grasslands, and other habitats that currently support far higher biodiversity than even the best-managed organic farmland. From this perspective, organic farming protects biodiversity locally while harming it globally.

texts.label: Nuclear essential for climate goals
texts.passage: Climate-policy analyses that include nuclear power among the technologies required to reach net-zero by 2050 tend to conclude that achieving deep emission cuts without nuclear is significantly harder and more expensive. The authors of these analyses argue that nuclear power produces very low life-cycle emissions, runs continuously rather than intermittently, and has an excellent safety record per unit of energy delivered when compared honestly with the harms of fossil-fuel air pollution. From this perspective, opposition to nuclear power imposes a real cost on climate goals.

texts.label: Nuclear too slow and costly
texts.passage: Critics of expanded nuclear power argue that new nuclear plants typically take 10 to 15 years to build, run well over their original budgets, and arrive too late to deliver the emission cuts that the climate timeline demands. The same critics argue that the unit cost of new nuclear has risen even as the unit cost of solar and wind has fallen substantially, and that on a strict pounds-per-tonne-of-CO2-avoided basis, money is better spent on renewables, storage, and grid upgrades than on new nuclear capacity. From this perspective, nuclear is not anti-climate but economically uncompetitive in the time window that matters.

texts.label: WFH raises productivity
texts.passage: Several large-scale studies of remote work, conducted during and after the 2020-22 pandemic, report that well-supported remote work is associated with measurable productivity gains for many knowledge-work roles. Workers report fewer interruptions, longer focused working blocks, time saved on commuting, and greater control over their working environment. The authors argue that, where the work itself does not require physical presence, remote work is a positive-sum change for both workers and employers.

The authors argue that, where the work itself does not require physical presence, remote work is a positive-sum change for both workers and employers.

texts.label: WFH harms collaboration and juniors
texts.passage: A different strand of research on remote work reports that productivity effects depend strongly on the type of work and the experience of the worker. Junior employees who lack established networks, complex collaborative projects requiring tight informal coordination, and creative work that benefits from spontaneous conversation all suffer in fully-remote settings. Several large technology firms have reduced remote-work options on the basis of these concerns, citing slower mentoring, weaker team coherence, and reduced innovation as the reasons.

texts.label: Lower voting age beneficial
texts.passage: Studies of jurisdictions that have lowered the voting age to 16 — Austria, Scotland for its 2014 independence referendum, and several others — report that 16- and 17-year-old voters turn out at high rates and engage seriously with the issues. Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among 16- and 17-year-olds in Scotland's 2014 referendum was substantially higher than among 18- to 24-year-olds, and that habits formed at 16 appear to persist. The authors argue that early enfranchisement strengthens democratic participation over the long term.

texts.label: Lower voting age premature
texts.passage: Critics of votes at 16 argue that the relevant question is not whether 16-year-olds can vote competently in isolated cases but whether the cognitive and life-experience benchmarks that justify other adult thresholds — driving, military service, drinking, contracts — also justify voting. The critics observe that several of these thresholds are higher than 16 in most jurisdictions, that the case for voting at 16 rests on participation evidence rather than competence evidence, and that the same participation gains might be achievable through stronger civic education without changing the formal voting age.

texts.label: Paper reading produces deeper comprehension
texts.passage: Studies in reading-research journals have compared comprehension among teenagers reading the same texts on paper or on a screen, with paper readers tending to score higher on retention questions after a delay. The authors of these studies argue that the linear, undistracted nature of paper reading supports deeper processing, and that print should remain the default medium for sustained academic reading even where screen alternatives are cheaper and more easily distributed.

texts.label: Screen reading equivalent when designed well
texts.passage: A more recent body of research argues that screen-reading effects depend heavily on screen design, font choice, and reader experience, and that well-designed digital reading apps produce comprehension comparable to print. The authors note that earlier studies often compared print with poorly designed websites or PDFs scrolled on small phone screens — not equivalent conditions — and that the apparent paper advantage shrinks or disappears in like-for-like comparisons. From this perspective, the medium is less important than the design quality and the reader's habits.

texts.title: The case for compulsory cycling infrastructure
texts.passage:
Every year, the same headlines return: another cyclist killed by a heavy goods vehicle on a city street, another inquest, another statement of regret. And every year, the same well-meaning advice circulates: wear a helmet, wear hi-vis, take the route the council recommends. The advice is not wrong. But it is also not enough.

Consider the Netherlands. Consider Denmark. Consider, increasingly, parts of Belgium, parts of Germany, parts of Spain. What do these countries have in common? Not compulsory helmet laws. Not unusually careful drivers. Not magically law-abiding cyclists. What they have is infrastructure — protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by kerbs and bollards, designed for ordinary people on ordinary bikes going at ordinary speeds. Where this infrastructure exists, cycling-injury rates are among the lowest in the world. Where it does not, the inquests continue.

The argument that personal protective equipment is the answer puts the responsibility on the cyclist. But the cyclist is not the problem. The problem is that cyclists and lorries share the same strip of tarmac, separated by nothing more substantial than a painted white line. The painted white line does not stop a thirty-tonne vehicle that has drifted half a metre out of its lane. Infrastructure does.

We accept this principle in almost every other area of public safety. We do not tell pedestrians to wear armour and trust their reflexes when crossing a motorway; we build pedestrian bridges. We do not tell swimmers to be careful around boats in a harbour; we forbid swimming there. We do not tell children to watch for traffic outside their classroom; we put up barriers and lower the speed limit. We accept that, in the design of public space, the heavier and faster vehicle must be the one constrained, not the lighter and more vulnerable user.

Yet on roads, the same principle is reversed. The lighter and more vulnerable user is told to wear plastic on their head. The heavier vehicle is given the lane. This is not safety policy. This is the appearance of safety policy, designed to make the absence of real action feel like activity.

Helmets help in individual crashes. The evidence is clear on that. But individual helmets do not stop the next inquest, because helmets do not change the conditions that produce inquests. Conditions are changed by design. Roads are conditions. Roads are designed. The question is not whether the cyclist is wearing the right equipment. The question is whether the road is.

The Netherlands made its choice fifty years ago, after a year in which four hundred and fifty children died on its roads. They built the infrastructure. We have not. Every year that we do not, we choose. And every year that we choose, another inquest waits.

texts.title: Against the digitisation of the classroom
texts.passage:
Walk into a state-of-the-art classroom in any wealthy country and you will see the same thing: rows of children in front of glowing rectangles. The rectangles are praised. They are interactive. They are engaging. They are the future. They are also, increasingly, evidence that we have got something seriously wrong.

Consider what learning actually requires. It requires sustained attention. It requires the ability to hold an idea in mind long enough to do something difficult with it. It requires, sometimes, the willingness to be bored, because boredom is what teaches the mind to settle. None of these conditions are easy to create at the best of times. They are nearly impossible to create on a device specifically designed by the world's most profitable companies to capture, hold, and resell the user's attention by any means available.

We are not naive about this in other contexts. We do not let children gamble. We do not let them drink. We are increasingly cautious about what we let them eat. We accept, in those domains, that adult judgment must override the child's preference, because the child's preference is being manipulated by industries with the resources to manipulate it well. Yet we hand them, at the age of eleven, the device that the gambling, drinking, and food industries can only dream of: one they will use willingly, for hours each day, that knows their face and their friends and exactly which colours light up which part of their reward system.

And we put it in the classroom. We tell them it is for learning. We are surprised when test scores drop. We are surprised when attention spans shorten. We are surprised when teachers report that pupils struggle to read three pages of continuous prose without checking something else.

The defenders of classroom digitisation point to the genuine educational uses of technology — and there are some. A spreadsheet for a science investigation is a useful tool. A coding environment for a computer-science lesson is a useful tool. A controlled, time-limited research session for a specific question is a useful tool. These uses are not what fills the average classroom screen. What fills the average classroom screen is what fills every other screen in the child's life: notifications, half-finished thoughts, the gentle ache of interruption that we have all come to accept as the price of being conscious in our century.

There is no special version of the device that switches off the parts that hurt learning when the school day begins. There is just the device, doing what it was designed to do, in a room where it was not designed to be.

Schools that have removed phones from classrooms tend to report what one might predict: a quieter room, longer attention on a single task, easier teacher-led discussion, calmer corridors at break. These are not small things. These are the substrate of education. We removed it. We can put it back.

texts.title: Why universal public services matter
texts.passage:
There is a recurring argument in policy circles about whether public services should be universal — available to everyone, regardless of income — or targeted to those who need them most. On the surface, targeting sounds more efficient. Why should a millionaire's children attend a free state school? Why should a wealthy commuter ride a subsidised train? Surely it is better to focus the available money on those whose need is greatest.

The surface argument is wrong. It is wrong not because targeting is theoretically misguided but because, in practice, every country that has tried to build a welfare system on targeting alone has discovered the same structural problem. Targeted services tend to deteriorate, because their users have little political power to defend them. Universal services tend to be defended, because they are used by everybody, including the people whose voices count most loudly in political life.

The classic illustration is the British National Health Service. The NHS is universal. It is also, despite every attempt to weaken it, persistently popular and persistently defended. By contrast, services that are available only to those below an income threshold tend to acquire stigma, attract press hostility, and lose funding in successive budget rounds. The very people they were designed to help end up using services that have been steadily hollowed out by politicians who do not personally rely on them.

There is a second, equally important reason for universality, which targeting advocates often miss. Targeted services impose costs on their users that universal services do not. To receive a targeted benefit, the user must prove eligibility, fill in forms, attend interviews, and accept the surveillance that follows. The cost of administering this gate-keeping is itself substantial. The cost to the user — in time, in stigma, in lost earnings during interviews, in failed claims — is often higher than the value of the benefit itself. Universal services impose none of these costs. The child enrols at the local school. The patient walks into the local hospital. There is no questionnaire, no interview, no proof, no shame.

Defenders of targeting will reply that universal services are wasteful — that we are spending public money on people who do not need it. This is true in the narrow sense and misleading in the broad sense. We do spend some universal-service money on people who could afford to pay privately. We also collect tax from those same people at a level that more than offsets what they receive. The net flow runs in the direction of redistribution; the universal form simply protects the recipients from the indignities of having to prove themselves worthy.

Universal public services are not inefficient. They are politically self-defending, administratively simple, and equitable in their treatment of every user. The case for them is not sentimental. It is structural. It is why the countries with the most resilient welfare states are also, almost without exception, the countries whose welfare states are built on universal foundations.

texts.title: In defence of boredom
texts.passage:
We have decided, as a culture, that boredom is bad. Boredom is something to be defended against. We carry, in every pocket, a device whose primary purpose is to ensure that we are never bored again — that no moment of queuing, of waiting, of being briefly alone with ourselves, ever has to be tolerated.

This was not always the case. Within living memory, ordinary life contained substantial unfilled time. The queue at the post office. The wait for the bus. The half hour between dinner and bedtime when there was nothing in particular to do. Children grew up with hours of empty Sunday afternoons. Adults walked to work without a podcast in their ears. None of this was experienced as deprivation. It was, simply, what time felt like when there was nothing to fill it.

What did people do during this unfilled time? They thought. They noticed. They had ideas. They had the unstructured, unpurposeful, slightly tedious moments out of which most creative thought, most planning, most self-knowledge, and a great deal of good conversation has historically emerged. Boredom, in other words, was not a state to be eliminated. It was a state in which other states became possible.

The cultural assumption that all of this can simply be replaced by entertainment is one of the strangest experiments of our century. We have not stopped to ask whether the human mind needs unfilled time the way the body needs sleep. We have not paused to wonder whether the disappearance of boredom, since around 2007, might be related to the simultaneous appearance of a great many disorders of attention, mood, and creative production that did not exist on the same scale before.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

It is true that boredom is uncomfortable. It is true that the mind initially resists it the way the body initially resists exercise. But discomfort is not the same as harm. The discomfort of boredom is the discomfort of a faculty stretching against the limits of its current state — and that stretching is, in every domain we understand, how the faculty grows. We do not stop a child from doing hard maths because the child finds it hard. We should not stop a mind from being bored because the mind finds boredom hard.

The cure for boredom is not entertainment. The cure for boredom is the mind itself, given time to do what it does when no one is asking it to perform. We have built a culture that almost never gives the mind that time. We are, predictably and at scale, less creative, less reflective, and less at home in our own heads than the generations that grew up with unfilled afternoons.

Put the device down. Sit for ten minutes. Be bored. It is not a deficit. It is a deep human capacity that has been quietly retreating since the year the smartphone arrived. We can call it back.

texts.topic: Should phones be removed from secondary classrooms?

paragraphs.text: Phones in classrooms have become one of the most divisive issues in modern education. This essay argues that secondary schools should remove phones from classrooms during lesson time, because the educational costs of in-class phone use outweigh the limited benefits and because well-designed removal policies have been shown to support pupil focus and reduce inequality of attention.

Removing phones from classrooms improves concentration. Beland and Murphy's 2015 LSE Centre for Economic Performance working paper on phone bans reported modest test-score gains in schools that introduced bans, with the largest gains for lower-attaining pupils. This finding suggests that phone removal is not merely a discipline measure but a measure that disproportionately helps pupils whose home circumstances already make focused study harder.

Furthermore, phones cause anxiety. Constant notifications keep pupils in a state of low-level alert that interrupts their thinking. Many pupils report that they feel calmer when their phones are not nearby. This is a clear reason to remove phones from classrooms during lessons.

Some educators argue that outright phone bans ignore the genuine educational uses of personal devices, including translation for language learners and accessibility tools. However, structured policies that use lockable pouches at the school entrance permit phones to be retrieved when their educational use is specifically required, and head teachers report that this approach is easier to enforce than partial in-class rules.

Removing phones from classrooms during lesson time is a proportionate measure with documented educational benefits. The policy supports pupil focus, particularly for lower-attaining pupils, and structured implementations using lockable pouches address the legitimate educational uses of devices without permitting the in-class distractions that are the principal cost. Secondary schools should adopt the policy.

texts.topic: Should secondary school start times be moved to 8:30 a.m. or later?

paragraphs.text: Adolescent sleep is a documented public-health issue. This essay argues that secondary schools should move their start times to no earlier than 8:30 a.m., on the grounds that the policy is supported by adolescent biology, by attendance and crash outcomes in changed districts, and by the recommendations of major public-health bodies.

The biology of adolescent sleep is well documented. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., citing the adolescent shift in circadian rhythms that makes very early start times incompatible with the sleep teenagers actually need. This is a recommendation from a major public-health body grounded in the underlying biology of the age group.

School cafeterias often serve unhealthy food at lunchtime. Many pupils choose chips, sweets, and sugary drinks over balanced options. Schools should offer healthier choices and provide nutrition education to support good eating habits.

Some district administrators argue that bus rotations and after-school sport make later start times logistically impossible. However, districts that have made the shift report that initial transport-restructuring costs are typically absorbed within one to two academic years, and that the wellbeing improvements outweigh the early administrative burden.

Secondary schools should adopt 8:30 a.m. start times. This change would also be a good moment to introduce mandatory meditation in all morning lessons, which would further support pupil wellbeing. The combined policy would represent a significant improvement in secondary education.

texts.topic: Should single-use plastics be banned in retail?

paragraphs.text: Single-use plastic waste is a documented environmental problem with measurable consequences for marine and terrestrial ecosystems. This essay argues that retail single-use plastics should be banned, on the grounds that voluntary measures have not worked, that the policy has been successfully implemented elsewhere, and that the costs of inaction are larger than the costs of the ban.

Bans on single-use plastic items have been successfully implemented in several jurisdictions. After Ireland introduced a small charge on plastic bags in 2002, bag consumption fell by over 90 percent within a year and the country reported a noticeable improvement in roadside litter. Similar measures in EU member states have also produced measurable reductions in plastic bag use.

Voluntary recycling has not worked. A recent report on global plastic waste found that only a tiny share of plastic produced each year is actually recycled, with the majority sent to landfill, incinerated, or leaked into the environment. This shows that voluntary measures alone cannot solve the problem.

Banning single-use plastics would help. The plastic that does not get used does not need to be cleaned up. The plastic that does not get used does not end up in the ocean. The plastic that does not get used does not need to be recycled. This is the cleanest possible outcome.

Retail single-use plastics should be banned. The policy has been successfully implemented elsewhere, voluntary alternatives have proven insufficient, and the environmental costs of continued use exceed the inconvenience of the transition. Bans are not the only tool, but they are the tool that consistently produces measurable change.

texts.topic: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?

paragraphs.text: The voting age sets a boundary between civic childhood and civic adulthood. This essay argues that the voting age should be lowered to 16, on the grounds of evidence from jurisdictions that have made the change, the formation of lasting voting habits at that age, and the precedent that 16-year-olds already carry many other adult responsibilities.

Evidence from jurisdictions that have lowered the voting age supports the case. Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among 16- and 17-year-olds in Scotland's 2014 independence referendum was substantially higher than turnout among 18- to 24-year-olds, and that habits formed at 16 appear to persist into adulthood. Similar findings have emerged from Austria, which has had a voting age of 16 for national elections since 2007.

Building on the evidence above, it is worth noting that the voting habit is itself a learned behaviour. Research on voter participation has consistently reported that people who vote in their first eligible election are more likely to vote in subsequent elections, while those who miss their first eligible election are less likely to start. A voting age of 16 means that the first eligible election typically coincides with school-based civic education, increasing the chance that the habit is established.

Critics of votes at 16 argue that the cognitive and life-experience benchmarks that justify other adult thresholds — driving, military service, contracts — also apply to voting. However, voting requires neither the physical coordination of driving nor the legal exposure of contract signing; it requires the ability to weigh competing arguments and apply civic-education knowledge, capacities that the evidence from Scotland and Austria suggests are present at 16.

Lowering the voting age to 16 is supported by participation evidence from jurisdictions that have made the change, by the formation of lasting voting habits at that age, and by the inadequacy of the competing thresholds as a reason against. The change is not transformative on its own, but it is a modest and defensible reform whose evidence base has continued to grow.

texts.topic: Should cycle infrastructure be mandatory in all UK city plans?

paragraphs.text: Cycle safety is a public-policy question with measurable consequences. This essay argues that protected cycle infrastructure should be a mandatory component of all UK city plans, on the grounds of comparative evidence from countries with the safest cyclists, the limits of individual protective equipment as a substitute, and the documented cost-effectiveness of infrastructure investment.

Cross-country comparisons of cyclist-safety outcomes suggest that countries with the safest cycling environments tend to combine well-designed protected infrastructure, lower urban speed limits, and strong driver-awareness norms. The Netherlands and Denmark, both with very high cycling rates and very low cycling-injury rates, have made protected infrastructure a standard feature of urban planning rather than an optional extra.

Climate change is also an important reason for cities to take cycling seriously. The transport sector is one of the largest sources of CO2 emissions in the UK, and modal shift from cars to bikes would contribute to national emission-reduction targets. Cycling is also good for personal health and reduces NHS costs.

Critics of mandatory cycle infrastructure argue that the cost is too high and that road space is too limited in older UK cities. However, evaluations of UK schemes including London's protected Cycleway network indicate that the cost per casualty avoided compares favourably with other safety interventions, and that the share of urban road space already devoted to private-car parking is substantial enough to accommodate redesign in most cities.

Mandatory cycle infrastructure in UK city plans is supported by comparative evidence, by the limits of individual protective equipment as a substitute, and by the documented cost-effectiveness of infrastructure schemes. The change would be substantial but achievable, and the alternative — repeating the cycle-fatality patterns of the past — has no defensible justification.

texts.topic: Should public services be universal rather than targeted?
texts.draft:
(1) Universal services are better than targeted ones. (2) Targeted services have a structural problem: their users typically have less political power to defend them when budgets are cut. (3) Universal services tend to be defended because everyone uses them. (4) This is just how things are.

(5) There is a second reason for universality. (6) Targeted services impose costs on their users — proving eligibility, filling in forms, attending interviews — that universal services do not. (7) These costs are often higher than the value of the benefit itself. (8) Targeting is bad.
texts.sourceContext: Research on welfare-state design has consistently reported that universal services prove politically more resilient than targeted ones, and that the administrative costs of targeting — both for the state and for the user — can be substantial. The British NHS is widely cited as an example of a universal service that has retained both political support and funding through repeated reform efforts.
